sentences.text: A mapmaker opened a wide drawer and found a map that did not match the modern streets.
The paper was soft at the folds, and the ink had faded to a brown whisper.
The river on the old map bent in the same place as the river outside the window.
A bridge was drawn there too, but the mapmaker knew the current bridge stood a mile upstream.
Curious, the mapmaker copied the old bend onto a fresh sheet and walked down to the river.
Willows leaned over the water. There was no bridge, only a tumble of cut stones in the shallows.
The stones were squared, not like ordinary river rocks, and moss grew on their flat tops.
They lined up with the two banks, as if they had once reached toward each other.
The mapmaker knelt, measured the gap with a length of string, and compared it with the old drawing.
The gap matched the width of the bridge on the old map.
Those stones were the feet of a bridge the town no longer used.
Back at the desk, the mapmaker added a note to the new map: old bridge base, seen at low water.
The modern streets stayed as they are. The past was added as a careful note, not as a guess.
A map can be out of date for today and still tell the truth about yesterday.
The test is to check the drawing against the ground before believing every line.

questions.prompt: What is this story mostly about?

choices.text: Building a new bridge a mile upstream in one day
Checking an old map against the river before trusting it
Throwing away every map that looks old
Moving the river so it matches a drawing

questions.explanation: The mapmaker notices a mismatch, walks to the river, measures, and only then writes a note. Testing the map is the main idea.

questions.prompt: Where is the current bridge compared with the old drawing?

choices.text: A mile out to sea
Under the mapmaker's desk
A mile upstream
On top of the willows

questions.explanation: The story says the current bridge stands a mile upstream from the bridge drawn on the old map.

questions.prompt: The ink had faded. What does faded mean here?

choices.text: Become brighter than new ink
Turned into a river bend
Been copied onto a fresh sheet
Grown faint with age

questions.explanation: Faded means grown faint. The ink has become a brown whisper on soft, folded paper, which shows age rather than fresh color.

questions.prompt: Why do the squared stones matter?

choices.text: They are not ordinary rocks, and their gap matches the old bridge
They prove the river was drawn backward
They show the current bridge is still in that spot
They mean the mapmaker measured the wrong bend

questions.explanation: Ordinary river rocks are not squared, and these stones line up with the banks. The matching width is another clue that they belonged to the old bridge.

questions.prompt: What does the mapmaker do first after copying the bend?

choices.text: Measures the gap with string
Walks down to the river
Writes a note on the new map
Decides the streets must be redrawn

questions.explanation: Copying the bend leads straight to the walk. Measuring and writing the note happen after the mapmaker is at the river.
